list.listitem: Ehrlichiosis is a serious rickettsial disease transmitted by the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum) and the blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis); cases have been reported in most states. C

Early clinical diagnosis is difficult and is based on risk of exposure, clinical features (flu-like illness, fever, headache, myalgia, malaise, rash), and laboratory testing. Rash is much less common than in Rocky Mountain spotted fever. C
Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, mild hyponatremia, and mildly elevated hepatic transaminase levels are common. C
Treat with doxycycline 100 mg po bid in adults and 2.2 mg/kg in children weighing less than 45 kg.B

background.definition: Ehrlichiosis is a serious tickborne disease, transmitted by the bite of hard-bodied (ixodid) ticks. Disease is caused by the bacteria Ehrlichia chaffeensis, E. ewingii, or E. muris eauclairensis in the United States. E. chaffeensis contributes to majority of the cases. and is also called human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis because the major target cell is monocytes. E. ewingii targets granulocytes and causes human granulocytotropic anaplasmosis.

list.listitem: Ehrlichiosis is most frequently reported in the southeastern and south-central United States, from the East Coast extending westward to Texas according to CDC . C
In 2018, four states (Missouri, Arkansas, New York, and Virginia) accounted for more than half of all reported cases of ehrlichiosis as per CDC.
During 2001 to 2002, the reported annual incidence was 0.7 cases per million.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there has been a 9-fold increase in ehrlichiosis (200 cases in the year 2000, increasingto 1,799 cases in 2018) but the case fatality has declined and is now 1% of cases.
Ehrlichia chaffeensis and Ehrlichia ewingii, transmitted by the lone star tick (A. americanum).
See map in for distribution in the United States.
The incubation period is 5 to 10 days. Tickborne rickettsial diseases are clinically similar but have distinct cell tropisms.
Rickettsiae cause small-vessel vasculitis, which manifests in skin rash, or as organ involvement in the brain or lungs.
E. chaffeensis infects monocytes and E. ewingii infects granulocytes.
Rickettsiae multiply in cytoplasmic membrane-bound vacuoles as microcolonies called morulae, which may occasionally be seen in leukocytes stained with Wright or Giemsa stains.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Illness in family member or exposed acquaintance

list.listitem: The key to prevention is to prevent tick bites by limiting exposure to tick habitats, including grassy and wooded areas. C
Use tick repellants on skin and permethrin on clothing. C
Inspect the body carefully for ticks after being in a tick habitat. C
Remove attached ticks immediately by grasping with tweezers close to the skin and pulling gently with steady pressure. C
Patients present with a febrile illness 1-2 weeks after a tick bite, accompanied by weakness, headache, malaise, arthralgias and myalgias, nausea, and vomiting.C
Order CBC and peripheral smear to look for morulae, as well as a metabolic profile. C
A rise in antibody titers in serum samples obtained 2 to 3 weeks apart confirms ehrlichiosis. C

The CDC cautions that a diagnosis of ehrlichiosis should not be made without concurrent serologic assessment to exclude anaplasmosis. It also notes that ehrlichiosis is a nationally notifiable condition. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Rash 2 to 4 days after onset of fever, maculopapular or petechial, may be on palms and soles
Petechial rash from onset; abrupt onset
Petechiae on distal extremities; GC detectable in skin lesions
Blood smear shows fragmented RBCs, nucleated RBCs
Sulfonamides, aminopenicillins, phenytoin and other seizure medications, NSAIDS

list.listitem: Patients typically present with rapid onset of fever (96%), rigor, headache (72%), myalgia (68%), and malaise (77%). There is often a history of recreational or occupational activities with potential exposure to ticks in an endemic area within the previous 2 weeks. Symptoms are more severe in patients with immunosuppressive conditions and in the elderly. Children are more likely to report gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting or diarrhea.
The interval from tick bite to the onset of symptoms is typically 7 to 14 days (median 9 days).

In a case series of 228 patients in Minnesota and Wisconsin from the early 1990s, 98% had malaise, rigors, myalgias, and sweats, and 85% had headache. Fever was present in 100% but was part of the case definition.
Patients may present with lethargy, ataxia, slurred speech, and malaise, in addition to rash and cough.
A history of tick bite may be difficult to ascertain, since the bite is frequently painless, and undetectable bites from nymphs may transmit infection.

The rash may appear as diffuse erythema or be maculopapular or petechial. It involves the extremities, trunk, face, and, rarely, palms and soles. The rash is present in one-third of adults with ehrlichiosis (two-thirds of children); rash is rare in E. ewingii infection.
A case report described a patient with ehrlichiosis who presented with a syndrome resembling thrombotic thrombocyopenic purpura.
Severe presentation with ARDS, shock, renal or hepatic failure, and coagulopathy are possible.

Patients may have leukopenia (occurring in 58%) with a nadir of 1300 to 4000 cells/mcl, thrombocytopenia (occurring in 79%) with a nadir of 50,000 to 140,000 platelets/mcl, mild hyponatremia, and mildly elevated hepatic transaminase (occurring in 68%). CSF does not reliably distinguish from meningococcal disease.

Clinical illness precedes laboratory diagnosis; patients usually do not have diagnostic serum antibody titers during the first week of illness. The sensitivity of serologic tests increases as the illness progresses.
Blood smear microscopy may reveal the presence of morulae in infected leukocytes; they were seen in 80% of patients in a case series.
Paired serum samples obtained 2 to 3 weeks apart that demonstrate a rise in antibody titer confirm the diagnosis.

Whole blood specimens may be used for a PCR confirmation of ehrlichiosis; a negative result does not rule out the diagnosis. In a case series of 228 patients, only 43% had a positive PCR test for ehrlichiosis.

Consider ehrlichiosis in patients with rapid onset of fever, rigors, headache, myalgia, malaise, and rash within 2 weeks of recreational or occupational activities with potential exposure to ticks in an endemic area.
If the disease is suspected, order CBC and peripheral smear (to look for morulae [microcolonies of Ehrlichiae]), and a metabolic profile.
Give early empiric therapy when the epidemiologic and clinical features suggest ehrlichiosis or other rickettsial infection, such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever.C
Give doxycycline (100 mg twice a day for 7 days) in adults; 4 mg/kg/d divided every 12 hours in children. B

Doxycycline (100 mg twice a day for 7 days) is the drug of choice for the treatment of presumptive or confirmed ehrlichiosis in adults and children of all ages. Fever usually subsides within 2 days of starting doxycycline. The dose in children is 2.2 mg/kg twice daily for children weighing less than 45 kg. Antibiotics should be given for at least 3 days after fever has subsided and the patient is showing signs of clinical improvement. Other antibiotics (penicillins, sulfas, erythromycin) are ineffective.
While there had been concern about tooth staining with older tetracyclines, there is no evidence that doxycycline in children under age 8 years results in tooth staining.
Delay in treatment can lead to severe disease and a fatal outcome.
The CDC does not recommend routine use of antibiotics after a tick bite.
Add ceftriaxone when meningococcal infection cannot be ruled out.
Hospitalize patients with organ dysfunction, severe thrombocytopenia, mental status changes, and the need for supportive therapy.
ARDS is a rare complication.

There is a wide spectrum of disease, from mild and self-limited to severe. Severe manifestations of ehrlichiosis include renal failure, myocarditis, meningoencephalitis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, organ failure, and death. C
Mortality rate is 3% of patients with clinically evident ehrlichiosis.B

Complications are more common in immunocompromised persons. They include acute renal failure (34% immunocompromised vs 16% immunocompetent, acute respiratory distress syndrome (34% vs 20%), multi-organ failure (26% vs 15%) and secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (26% vs 15%).B
Delayed time to the initiation of therapy is an important risk factor for more severe disease and the need for ICU care.
Tetracyclines are warranted during pregnancy in life-threatening situations in which the clinical suspicion of ehrlichiosis is high.
A course of doxycycline does not pose a substantial threat of tooth staining in children.
The dose of doxycycline in children is 4 mg/kd/d divided every 12 hours and given orally or IV.
